meta.title: Who really said "This too shall pass"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a Bible verse. The saying is a Persian Sufi fable of a king's ring; its English form runs through Walter Scott (1813) and Edward FitzGerald (1852).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'This too shall pass'?
meta.ogDescription: 'This too shall pass' appears nowhere in the Bible. Its documented trail is Persian, then Scott's 1813 letter to Byron and FitzGerald's 1852 retelling.

answer.label: Not the Bible — a Persian Sufi fable
answer.authorDates: c. 1145 – c. 1221 · Persian Sufi poet who recorded the fable
answer.sourceLine: There is no such verse — the words appear nowhere in scripture. The saying is a Persian adage, carried in the fable of a king who asks his wise men for a motto that will hold true in prosperity and in ruin alike; Wikipedia’s survey places that ring story in the 12th-century Persian poets Sanai and Attar of Nishapur, and Jewish folklore retells it with Solomon as the sage. The English wording that actually got written down is not “this too shall pass” but “this also shall pass away” — the form Walter Scott used in a letter to Lord Byron on 6 November 1813 and Edward FitzGerald printed in 1852.

source.heading: The 1852 printing we could read

docMeta.dd: A Persian Sufi fable of a king’s consoling ring
Polonius: A Collection of Wise Saws and Modern Instances
Edward FitzGerald, 1852 (read here in the 1887 Works, p. 433)

source.excerpt:
SOLOMON’S SEAL.

The Sultan asked Solomon for a Signet motto, that should hold good for Adversity or Prosperity. Solomon gave him, “THIS ALSO SHALL PASS AWAY.”
trail: 12th century — The adage is traced to medieval Persian Sufi poetry; the fable of the king who asks his sages for a ring that will comfort him in sorrow, and receives one etched with these words, is recorded by Attar of Nishapur, whose Ilāhī-Nāma carries it ↗. The story also circulates in Jewish folklore, often with Solomon as the humbled king or the sage who delivers the line.

6 November 1813 — Walter Scott, writing to Lord Byron from Abbotsford, recalls “the Oriental tale… of a Sultan who consulted Solomon on the proper inscription for a signet-ring” and gives the maxim as “And this also shall pass away” ↗. He treats it as a story his correspondent will already know.

1852 — Edward FitzGerald prints the fable as “Solomon’s Seal” in Polonius: A Collection of Wise Saws and Modern Instances; this is the retelling that carried the adage into general English use. Read the scanned page in his collected Works ↗.

30 September 1859 — Abraham Lincoln quotes it to the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society in Milwaukee as the motto of an unnamed “Eastern monarch,” then argues for a prosperity that “shall not pass away” ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned page of Works of Edward FitzGerald (Houghton, Mifflin, 1887), p. 433, where Polonius is reprinted with its original 1852 date. Note the wording: “this also shall pass away,” not the five-word form quoted today. Scott’s letter to Byron of 6 November 1813 gives the same words — “And this also shall pass away” — and Lincoln’s 1859 version is “And this, too, shall pass away.”

source.rightsNote: Every text quoted on this page is long out of copyright in the United States: Walter Scott’s 1813 letter as published by Lockhart in the 1830s, Edward FitzGerald’s Polonius (1852, reprinted 1887), and Lincoln’s 1859 address — all first published well before 1931. The adage itself is anonymous folk material with no identifiable author or claimant, so no one holds rights in the sentence.

author.name: Attar of Nishapur
author.heading: Who was Attar of Nishapur?
author.metaLine: c. 1145 – c. 1221 · Persian Sufi poet and hagiographer of Nishapur
author.bio: Farid ud-Din Attar was a Persian poet, theoretician of Sufism and hagiographer from Nishapur, best known for The Conference of the Birds and the Memorial of the Saints; he shaped Persian mystical poetry and influenced Rumi directly. His Ilāhī-Nāma (“Book of God”), a poem of roughly 6,500 verses built from anecdotal tales, is where the fable of the king and the consoling ring is recorded. He is a transmitter here, not an author — the adage was already folk material moving through Persian and Jewish storytelling, and no single person can be shown to have coined it.

The documented English form is "this also shall pass away": Walter Scott to Lord Byron, 6 November 1813, and Edward FitzGerald, "Solomon's Seal," in Polonius (1852). Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most confidently mis-sourced sentences in English. Almost everyone who quotes it places it somewhere it has never been.

items.why: It is not a verse. The St. Paul Center is explicit: “Many people simply assume that the phrase comes from Sacred Scripture, but in fact it appears nowhere in the Bible” — the passages it gathers as biblical parallels are Matthew 24:35, 2 Corinthians 4:17–18 and Ecclesiastes 3 ↗, none of which contains this sentence.

In every early English telling Solomon is inside the story, not behind it. Scott’s 1813 letter describes “a Sultan who consulted Solomon on the proper inscription for a signet-ring,” and calls the result “the apophthegm supplied by the Jewish sage ↗” — a line of narrative fiction, not a citation.

Lincoln handled it honestly. At the Wisconsin State Fair on 30 September 1859 he prefaced it with “It is said an Eastern monarch once charged his wise men…” ↗, and then spent the rest of the passage arguing for something that would not pass away.

FitzGerald did put the adage into English circulation, but his 1852 text reads “THIS ALSO SHALL PASS AWAY ↗.” The compressed five-word form quoted today matches no early printed source we could locate.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody owns it. It is a Persian adage carried by a folk fable — recorded in 12th-century Persian Sufi poetry, retold in Jewish folklore with Solomon as the sage, and given its English shape by Walter Scott in 1813 and Edward FitzGerald in 1852 ↗, both of whom wrote “this also shall pass away.”

context.heading: Why the Bible gets the credit
lead: The adage sounds scriptural because everything around it is. In the story that carries it, the sage is King Solomon; the phrasing is King-James-shaped — “and this also shall pass away” — and the sentiment sits comfortably beside Ecclesiastes. Readers reach for the Bible because the sentence has been dressed in its clothes for two centuries.

But the trail runs east, not to Jerusalem. Wikipedia’s survey traces the specific phrase to medieval Persian Sufi poets and the fable of a king who commissions a ring motto that will steady him in triumph and in disaster; the same story circulates in Jewish folklore, sometimes compressed to the Hebrew initials for Gam zeh ya’avor. When Walter Scott passed it to Byron in 1813 he called it, precisely, “the Oriental tale.”
context.detailsSummary: What Lincoln actually did with it
detailsBody: Abraham Lincoln used the line at the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society fair in Milwaukee on 30 September 1859, and he introduced it as borrowed goods: “It is said an Eastern monarch once charged his wise men to invent him a sentence, to be ever in view, and which should be true and appropriate in all times and situations. They presented him the words: ‘And this, too, shall pass away.’”

He then argued against it. Lincoln granted the maxim its power — “How chastening in the hour of pride! — how consoling in the depths of affliction!” — before reaching for something he hoped would outlast it: a prosperity “which, while the earth endures, shall not pass away.” He is quoted today for a sentence he was pushing back on.
context.pull: Solomon is a character in the story, not the author of it.

sourcesVerified.claim: The phrase is an adage of likely Persian origin, is sometimes mistaken for a Biblical passage, appears in the 12th-century works of Sanai and Attar of Nishapur (Attar records the ring fable), appears in Jewish folklore often with Solomon, and reached English via Scott's 1813 letter to Byron and FitzGerald's 1852 'Solomon's Seal' in Polonius.
The phrase 'this too shall pass' appears nowhere in the Bible; the article names Matthew 24:35, 2 Corinthians 4:17-18, Galatians 6:9 and Ecclesiastes 3 as conceptual parallels only.

Walter Scott's letter 'TO THE RIGHT HON. LORD BYRON', dated Abbotsford, 6th November 1813, recounts 'the Oriental tale... of a Sultan who consulted Solomon on the proper inscription for a signet-ring' and gives the apophthegm as 'And this also shall pass away.'
Project Gutenberg ebook 42062 is 'Memoirs of the Life of Sir Walter Scott, Volume 4 (of 10)' by J. G. Lockhart, the volume containing the 6 November 1813 letter to Byron.

Works of Edward FitzGerald (Houghton, Mifflin, 1887) reprints Polonius: A Collection of Wise Saws and Modern Instances (1852) and contains, at p. 433, the entry 'SOLOMON'S SEAL. The Sultan asked Solomon for a Signet motto, that should hold good for Adversity or Prosperity. Solomon gave him, "THIS ALSO SHALL PASS AWAY."'

Lincoln's address to the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society, Milwaukee, 30 September 1859, contains: 'It is said an Eastern monarch once charged his wise men to invent him a sentence... They presented him the words: "And this, too, shall pass away."' and later 'which, while the earth endures, shall not pass away.'
The English phrase 'this too shall pass' is a calque of Classical Persian this too shall pass (in niz bugzarad).
Attar of Nishapur was a Persian poet, theoretician of Sufism and hagiographer, c. 1145 - c. 1221, author of The Conference of the Birds and Memorial of the Saints, an influence on Rumi.
The Ilahi-Nama ('Book of God') is a 12th-century Persian poem by Farid ud-Din Attar of roughly 6,500 verses built from anecdotal stories.
Edward FitzGerald was an English poet and translator born 31 March 1809, died 1883.
